transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14 | Start: 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~47m
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (NovusHealth ML Eng), Ethan Brooks (Novus PM), Sandeep Rao (Novus Infra)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- We reviewed the last 48h runs: int8-small, int8-medium, fp8-blend variant.
- Noted a small quality delta on 'legal' workload (low frequency intents) and a throughput gain on int8 variants.
- Agreed on triage: export failing prompts, run a longer int8 spike with KV cache, and review infra/throughput constraints for private deploy.

Topics: Quality deltas; Latency/throughput numbers; KV/Prefix cache effects; Rollout/fallback; Security checklist (SOC2/KMS).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura: okay everyone, uh, thanks for joining — I think we have a full house, quick check on ankles, um attendees?
[00:05] Maya: Maya here, hi.
[00:07] Ethan: Ethan, yep.
[00:09] Sandeep: Sandeep on infra.
[00:11] Diego: Diego from Redwood, thanks.
[00:13] Laura: Cool. Quick agenda, we'll go through the 48 hour int8/fp8 runs, show the small heatmap, surface the 2-3 regression buckets, and agree next run — sound good?
[00:22] Ethan: Sounds good. Main thing for us is whether int8 gives us the throughput we need without surprising accuracy drops on legal Qs.
[00:29] Maya: yeah that legal cluster is our canary — low freq but high-stakes, even small hallucination increases are, uh, unacceptable.
[00:35] Diego: Totally — quick data first: from the 48h: int8-medium p95 lat went from baseline fp16 120ms down to ~88ms, that's about 27% improvement at p95. int8-small was 95ms p95 but with higher variance on longer contexts. fp8-blend sits around 100ms but shows slightly better quality on rare intents.
[00:52] Sandeep: Can you repeat the numbers, I missed the fp8?
[00:54] Diego: Sure — fp8-blend p95 ~100ms, int8-medium p95 ~88ms, fp16 baseline 120ms. Throughput measured in tokens/sec improved roughly 1.4x on int8-medium.
[01:08] Maya: And quality? what's the delta on our legal eval set?
[01:11] Diego: Right — on the 3k eval set: int8-medium shows a 1.6% drop in intent-level accuracy specifically concentrated on those 'legal' patterns, fp8-blend shows ~0.6% drop. Hallucination rate for int8 up about 0.7% from baseline. Those numbers are small but concentrated.
[01:30] Ethan: Okay, that's the nuance — small overall but dangerous where it matters. What's the error surface look like? are these paraphrase failures, tokenization, or something else?
[01:39] Diego: Preliminary look: most failures are around rare named entities and heavily nested clauses. We suspect quantization sensitivity in attention logits for very low-probability tokens. Also, KV cache interactions change scoring slightly on repeated contexts which can amplify or dampen outputs.
[01:55] Laura: On that KV cache note — last week's run had caching off for reproducibility, this week Diego added prefix cache for a subset. Any noticeable delta?
[02:03] Diego: Yes — enabling KV cache reduced overall latency by ~30% for repeated helpdesk contexts — p95 for cached paths dropped from 120ms to 85ms on fp16, and int8 cached p95 down to ~65ms. But caching also surfaced a small regression where the model re-used a stale key and repeated a wrong assert — it's subtle.
[02:24] Maya: Hmm, interesting. So cache helps latency but can change the distribution of outputs. That could explain some of the hallucination drift.
[02:30] Diego: Exactly. We're tracking both the per-query perplexity shift and ngram diffs to find systematic patterns.
[02:35] Ethan: Are we able to reproduce a failure locally against the same seed / context?
[02:39] Diego: Reproducibility is hit-or-miss because beam/temperature interactions plus micro-batching reorder ops. Some failures reproduced when we forced identical batch shapes and the same prefix cache state.
[02:52] Sandeep: From infra side, our big ask is: what RAM / GPU memory changes with int8 vs fp8? If we plan private deploys inside our VPC, we need to know instance sizing.
[03:02] Diego: Int8 roughly halves activation memory so you can fit ~1.8x to 2x more concurrency on same GPU. FP8 is similar but depends on kernel support — we used a mixed FP8 path that requires newer CUDA kernels, so on older infra int8 may be more portable.
[03:18] Sandeep: Noted. We have older A100 gen 1 boxes in one cluster, so FP8 with custom runtimes might be tricky.
[03:24] Maya: Back to quality — can we get a prioritized failing prompt list? I'd like the top 200 failing prompts with model outputs and reference.
[03:32] Diego: Yes, we can export that. We'll include the ngram diffs and token-level logits where available.
[03:38] Laura: Great. Next, fallback/rollout strategy: Diego, what's Redwood's recommended approach if we want to roll int8 into prod with safety?
[03:45] Diego: We recommend a staged rollout: 1) Canary on non-sensitive traffic with logging and auto rollback threshold; 2) Progressive ramp with mixed-routing — that is, route low-latency tolerant requests to int8, and high-risk requests to fp16/fp8; 3) If dataset-specific regressions show, enable a model-fallback rule that sends flagged intents to the baseline. We can implement routing policies in the Redwood control plane and attach eval hooks.
[04:10] Ethan: Mixed-routing sounds good. Can routing be based on intent classifier confidence?
[04:15] Diego: Yep — either a lightweight classifier or a confidence threshold on model output. Redwood's routing supports metadata-based rules, so you can tag requests and route accordingly.
[04:24] Sandeep: How about encryption and audit logs? We need SOC2 + KMS envelope for private deployment — is that available?
[04:30] Laura: Yes, for private deployment we provide KMS integrations and audit logs; we have a compliance pack which includes SOC2 scope. I'll share the checklist after call.
[04:38] Sandeep: Great, please include HSM notes if available.
[04:41] Laura: will do.
[04:43] Maya: small question — the examples where int8 failed, were they concentrated by prompt length?
[04:48] Diego: Good question — mostly longer prompts with nested clauses and some long context examples show amplified differences, probably due to accumulation of quant noise in attention. But we did see a few short prompts fail as well, particularly ones with rare tokens.
[05:01] Ethan: Any plan for a sensitivity sweep? i.e., run slices varying sequence length and temperature to map out fragile regions?
[05:07] Diego: Yes, that's part of the next-run plan: 1) sensitivity sweep across seq lengths [64,128,512], temps [0.0,0.4,0.8], and seeds; 2) run with and without KV cache; 3) produce per-slice SNR and accuracy deltas. We'll include a heatmap.
[05:25] Maya: timeline?
[05:27] Diego: We can queue the sweep if we get the eval subset today. The 6h short run will be done by EOD tomorrow, the 24h spike by Friday.
[05:36] Laura: Okay so action items — Diego will run an int8 spike with KV cache, Diego to export heatmaps; Maya will provide eval subset; Laura to share security docs. Anything else?
[05:45] Maya: I'll also annotate the top 50 edge-case intents manually to prioritize checks.
[05:49] Ethan: Can Redwood also run a mixed-precision path where only attention matmuls use fp8 and rest int8? Might be useful as a mitigation and to test tradeoffs.
[05:59] Diego: We experimented with hybrid kernels — they're possible but require extra compilation time. We can schedule a hybrid run as part of the 24h spike but it will cost extra GPU hours.
[06:10] Sandeep: Cost note — please surface estimated GPU hours for each run in the report, so we can align with budget.
[06:14] Laura: will include.
[06:16] Ethan: Also curious whether this is a vendor gap — mentioned Anthropic earlier. Are we seeing anything different from what other vendors report?
[06:24] Diego: Not directly comparable — other vendors' runtimes and kernels differ. Our data suggests quantization sensitivity is model + kernel specific; vendors might hide that behind model variants. We did call out Anthropic and OpenAI as competitors folks sometimes evaluate.
[06:39] Maya: for inspectability, can we get token-level logits for failures? That helps us debug if it's scoring or sampling.
[06:45] Diego: We'll include token logits for the top 200 failures; for larger exports we may provide sampled diffs due to storage.
[06:52] Laura: Let's surface final decision criteria: what are we agreeing to as 'go/no-go' thresholds?
[06:57] Ethan: From product: no more than 0.5% absolute increase in hallucination on the legal bucket; and regret-free latency improvement of at least 20% for interactive web flows.
[07:08] Maya: From ML: prioritize zero-regression on the top 100 legal prompts, otherwise block for further tuning.
[07:14] Diego: We'll map our passes to those thresholds.
[07:18] Sandeep: From infra: ensure the instance sizing and KMS config are validated before a private deploy.
[07:24] Laura: Okay — recap and next steps?
[07:27] Diego: Run list — int8-medium 6h (quick), int8-medium 24h (spike), hybrid fp8+int8 trial (part of spike). Export top 200 failures, ngram diffs, token logits for top failures. Include GPU-hour estimate.
[07:43] Maya: Customer will provide 500 labeled eval subset (focus on legal) and annotate top 50 edge cases.
[07:50] Laura: I'll send SOC2/KMS checklist, and a short doc on routing/fallback policies.
[07:55] Ethan: Schedule perf triage with infra next week — I'll propose times.
[07:59] Sandeep: we'll confirm our cluster compatibility and send instance details.
[08:03] Laura: thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with links to the heatmap and the run queue.
[08:08] Diego: thanks all.
[08:10] (meeting ends)
